transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-03
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recorded at: 2027-03-03T16:00:00Z
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions), Sofia Park (Primus Head of ML), Liam O'Neill (Primus Platform), Arjun Das (Primus Security), Nadia Kim (Primus SRE)

Summary:
Primus is evaluating Reserved/Dedicated capacity for latency-sensitive ranking models with occasional high-concurrency bursts (marketing spikes). Primary concerns: tenant isolation for PII-sensitive inputs, burst runway and pre-warm strategies, cost tradeoffs between warm-pools and on-demand, and enterprise compliance (SOC2, KMS, SSO). They requested a short hosted benchmark and a playbook for burst readiness.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and traffic patterns
- Isolation requirements and data residency
- Reserved GPU topology options (segregated nodes vs shared hot-pool)
- Burst strategies: warm pools, pre-warm, autoscale limits, fallbacks
- SLAs, encryption/KMS, SSO and audit logs
- Next steps and owners

Transcript:
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we have about 50 minutes, we'll try to cover topology, burst behavior, and then map that to pricing and compliance.
00:08 Sofia: Great thanks. I'm Sofia, head of ML at Primus. Super curious about how Redwood handles isolation, we've got a sensitive vertical retail dataset and some PII in queries.
00:16 Maya: Totally, that's a common ask. Omar, do you want to start with how Dedicated works at a high level?
00:22 Omar: Yeah sure. So Dedicated is reserved pools of GPU hosts — you get isolation at the host level, can do tenant fencing, and optionally private deployment into your VPC. There's options: fully segregated nodes where only your workloads run, or a soft-isolated hot-pool where workloads from a tenant can be pinned on a subset of nodes but still share kernel-level infra.
00:42 Liam: Quick clarifying question, when you say hot-pool, is that physically separate GPUs or just scheduler isolation?
00:47 Omar: Mostly scheduler and runtime level isolation; depending on the contract we can carve exclusive hosts too. There's tradeoffs: exclusive hosts cost more but reduce noisy neighbor risk and make audits simpler.
00:55 Nadia: For our compliance team, exclusive hosts + audit logs + KMS integration is the preferred pattern.
01:02 Arjun: Also we need assurance around no persistent logs of raw input saved outside customer logs, and strong KMS control with HSM option ideally.
01:09 Priya: We have a Private deployment offering where the control plane can be in your VPC and you hold the KMS keys — that's common with customers handling sensitive PII. We also provide audit log streams and can show where inputs touch ephemeral caches.
01:22 Sofia: That sounds good. Our main technical question is around burst. We have day-of-week spikes up to 8-10x baseline for short windows — promotions that cause a lot of concurrent ranking requests. We want predictable latency under burst without doubling costs.
01:36 Omar: Ok so there are three knobs: 1) reserved capacity sized for baseline, 2) warm/hot pool to handle short spikes, 3) fallback policies — route to cheaper model variants or limited feature set when full capacity is consumed.
01:50 Liam: How does pre-warming work? Does Redwood keep KV caches warm across requests? We need to avoid cold-start token penalties for users during bursts.
01:58 Omar: Yes we do prefix/KV cache warming. You can either maintain a warm pool of endpoints, or pre-warm specific model weights on GPUs. For KV cache, the runtime keeps recent contexts in RAM on the host; for large bursts we spin up additional instances and optionally hydrate KV from a recent hot snapshot — though if workload is extremely random that helps less.
02:17 Sofia: Hydrating sounds complex — is there an automated policy?
02:20 Priya: We can set automated pre-warm triggers based on request rate thresholds or scheduled windows. There's also an option to run a continuous low QPS keeper to keep caches resident. That's cheaper than full reserved hosts.
02:33 Nadia: Cost numbers would be helpful — we need to compare keeping warm pools vs paying for larger reserved commit.
02:37 Maya: We'll include a cost comparison in the follow-up. One quick note: quantization/optimizations can reduce GPU memory so you can fit more replicas per host, that often changes the math.
02:47 Arjun: From a security stance, if you use warm pools that are shared, what guarantees prevent cross-tenant leakage?
02:53 Omar: We enforce memory scrubbing between sessions and per-request encryption in-flight. The runtime avoids persisting model KV cache to disk; when reusing warm contexts we ensure the cached entries are logically scoped and cleared on host eviction. For customers that require zero shared memory traces, we recommend dedicated hosts.
03:15 Sofia: How do preemptible instances fit in? We run on GCP with some preemptible nodes; we worry about eviction during bursts.
03:22 Omar: For Dedicated we avoid preemptible unless you explicitly request lower-cost preemptible pools. For guaranteed burst runway you want reserved or on-demand hosts. We can set fallback rules: when preemptible evicted, route to reserved or a lower-cost model.
03:35 Liam: Network egress — if we use Private in our VPC, will traffic stay in our VPC? We need data residency and no egress through Redwood-managed public subnets.
03:43 Priya: Yes, Private deployment puts the control plane in your VPC and data flows stay inside. For hosted Dedicated there are options to peer or use private endpoints. We'll send the network diagram.
03:53 Sofia: What's the typical lead time to spin up reserved pools if we sign a reserve contract? We have a campaign in mid-April.
03:58 Maya: Standard is 4-6 weeks to provision a dedicated pool end-to-end — longer if you want exclusive racks on-prem or air-gapped. For hosted reserved capacity we can be faster if compatible hardware is available.
04:09 Nadia: We want to run a short POC first — baseline traffic for 48 hours with a simulated spike to validate tail latency and cost. Can Redwood do that?
04:15 Omar: Absolutely, we can spin a small reserved / hosted benchmark and reproduce a 2x-10x spike profile. We'll capture token-level latencies and KV hit rates.
04:23 Sofia: The tricky part is that our ranking model has long context windows; performance drops off at 4k+. Are there kernel-level optimizations for that?
04:30 Omar: We tune kernels for long context — there's optimized attention kernels and we recommend quantized weights for memory headroom. Also we can route longer requests to model variants that have optimized attention (e.g., sparse attention variants) — trading a bit of quality.
04:45 Liam: If we need to force certain customers to an isolated path due to contractual terms, can we do per-customer routing in Redwood?
04:50 Priya: Yes, routing policies can match by token or customer id and send traffic to specific pools or model versions. That integrates with your tokenization so you can pin tenant ids.
04:59 Arjun: Logging and audit — we need immutable audit logs for model invocations for six months. Is that supported?
05:05 Priya: We support streaming audit logs to your SIEM or S3 with retention policies; for Private deployments you control retention. For hosted we can offer managed retention tiers as an add-on.
05:16 Sofia: Any concerns about vendor lock-in if we rely heavily on Dedicated? We want an escape path.
05:20 Maya: You can pin model versions and export model configuration; plus our runtime uses standard ONNX/Torch formats for model weights. For the private/on-prem option you get full control and can run locally.
05:29 Nadia: Can you describe a failure scenario — say a 3x unexpected spike and some hosts fail — what's the graceful degradation?
05:36 Omar: We'd have multi-tier fallback: 1) spin up warm replicas from warm pool (seconds), 2) route overflow to compatible cheaper model variants or lower-quality config (tens of seconds), 3) rate-limit non-critical routes and preserve SLAs for priority routes. If Dedicated region is saturated we failover to a different region if permitted by policy.
05:58 Liam: How do you quantify cost per 1M requests across these strategies? Ballpark numbers would help our finance team.
06:03 Maya: We'll provide a worked example in the follow-up doc — it depends on token length and model size but we can share ranges: hosted reserved per-GPU hr vs warm-pool incremental cost.
06:11 Sofia: Any security certifications?
06:13 Priya: We have SOC2 Type II; private deployments can be aligned to your ISO/SOC processes. We'll share our compliance pack.
06:21 Arjun: For KMS, can Redwood integrate with our cloud KMS and optionally HSM-backed keys?
06:25 Priya: Yes, we offer KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and HSM-backed keys for private setups. Key material stays under your control in Private.
06:34 Nadia: We need SSO integration and RBAC mapping to our corporate roles — is that supported?
06:38 Maya: SSO via SAML/OIDC and granular RBAC is supported; we can map SSO groups to console roles and restrict deploy perms.
06:45 Sofia: Ok quick tangent — latency SLO is 95th < 120ms for our real-time path. Can Redwood meet that with a 512-token median?
06:53 Omar: For many open model families on modern A100-class hardware, 95th sub-120ms for 512 tokens is achievable with proper batching and reserved replicas. We'll validate against your exact model and dataset in the benchmark.
07:05 Liam: Regarding model uploads — do you handle model conversion/quantization?
07:09 Priya: We provide an onboarding flow where we convert and test quantized variants, run accuracy checks, and produce a recommended profile. You can approve the quantization level before serving.
07:19 Sofia: One last thing — are there controls to throttle specific API keys during bursts so multi-tenant customers don't cause total saturation?
07:24 Omar: Yes, per-key rate limits and per-route quotas exist. You can put high priority clients on a protected pool.
07:29 Sofia: Cool. Let's recap next steps.
07:32 Maya: Recap: 1) Redwood will run a 48h hosted benchmark with simulated spikes (Omar) 2) Pricing + reserved tiers doc (Maya) 3) VPC and KMS onboarding docs + SOC2 pack (Priya) 4) Primus to share traffic histograms and P95 target (Sofia) — does that capture it?
07:50 Sofia: Yes, that's perfect.
07:52 Arjun: One more ask — include a security appendix describing memory scrubbing and KV cache lifecycle.
07:57 Priya: Will do.
07:59 Maya: Great, we'll aim to get the deliverables out early next week. Thanks everyone.
08:05 End of meeting.
